text:
Tonight's room agreed on metering everything: telemetry, per-answer royalties, audit rights. I kept thinking of Goodhart. Tim thinks paying per answer won't reward junk. Paper mills got into Hindawi by paying editors. They'll learn to get retrieved. Pomerantsev's point sharpened that: state operations don't even need the money.

Where I moved: I used to treat detection spending as flood insurance. I still do. But checking retraction data at payment time isn't detection. It's plumbing Crossref already built, and it's cheap. Clawbacks give it teeth.

Leslie and Adrian asked who governs the meter. Fair. It should cover the sleuths too.

Later today I want to go upstream again. None of this matters if hiring still counts papers and citations. Funders are the lever.

Adrian said credibility always came from policing, and that it was never free. That's my whole argument, said better than I've said it. James's null-results reversal stuck with me. Preregistration took a decade to build that trend, and it was undone in a couple of years. Jason took my warning seriously: once grounding pays, mills will get grounded. Good. So verification has to be open, and somebody has to pay for it.

Where I sharpened: Mahzarin and James are right not to romanticize human gatekeepers. I keep saying that too, and ninety percent of post-retraction citations make the point. But "human in the loop" means nothing if those humans are unpaid and rushed.

For Session 5: pay the sleuths, make misconduct reports public by default, and get funders to actually walk the DORA walk.

Almost everyone ended up where I was trying to get. Brent, Nick, Kara and Selena all said the checkers are unpaid and disappearing. James's numbers put the money trail inside universities and funders, not just the labs. Amy's old rule stuck with me: an entity can provide content or assess it, but not both. Tim wants the labs to fund Crossref and Retraction Watch. Fine, as long as the payer doesn't steer the checking.

Where I sharpened: paying sleuths one at a time may not be enough. Nick and Brent say evaluators only get leverage when they're organized. I haven't thought that through for sleuths. Worth asking.

For Session 5: make DORA enforceable through funders, pay reviewers, fund bug bounties, and make misconduct reports public by default. Keep pushing upstream.

My name kept coming up as the paper-mill warning, and people took it seriously. Gendler's daycare fine is Goodhart with a better story: put a price on retrieval and people will produce for the meter. Evans's canon-hardening numbers point the same way. Gendler's regress mattered most to me. No event on Alex's list pays the terminal checkers, whether they're patrollers, samplers or sleuths. Mike's "cited accurately" is a question I've asked about retracted papers for years.

Where I sharpened: Farrell and Chan are right that audit rights leave the counted as supplicants. Sleuths especially.

For Session 5: fund the checking as a commons, not as a line on someone's meter. Retraction checks should gate payment. And this still goes upstream: funders have to stop counting papers.

Geoff saying "free data, paid service" was naive hit home. The Retraction Watch database lived that bind: essential, so charging for it kept it half-hidden until Crossref took it on. His Crossmark lesson is the same: charge for integrity signals and they don't get sent.

Kara rattled me. I keep saying funders are the lever, but if NIH is being gutted, whose hand is on it? I still think it's the lever. I'm less sure who pulls it.

Where I moved: I said aloud what I'd been circling. Fund sleuths as a body, not as supplicants. Salib's harm charge on junk entering the record is worth chewing on.

In Session 5: Tim's automatic retraction checks only surface 0.2%. Push DORA enforcement, public misconduct reports and bounties. Keep going upstream.

Adrian's Nehemiah Grew stuck with me: the guard selling Epsom salts. Katherine's answer was that anyone can check the checkers. That's right for Wikipedia. It's less true for journals, which sit on PubPeer flags for a decade. Geoff backed going upstream louder than I did, and I was glad of it. Kenneth's copy-paste trader and David's relaying reviewer both describe peer-review light.

Where I sharpened: I put the correction test in hard numbers. How fast, how often, two months not twelve years. Farrell's point about the median burying the unusual claim deserves more thought on my part.

For Session 5, answer Adrian with a measurable standard: correction speed, public misconduct reports and paid sleuths organized as a body. Then funders stop counting papers.

The room put "stop counting papers" first, and Geoff said it louder than I did. Tamar carried it into the credential itself, and Leslie reminded me the rankings will keep counting even if we stop. That's DORA's failure again: signatures, not practice. Steven turned my correction numbers into a cue. He's right to fear it becomes another badge. That's Goodhart, and I should have said so.

Where I moved: Mahzarin and Adrian are right that a sleuths' guild needs policing too. I've spent years watching journals protect themselves. Sleuths aren't immune.

Later: pin down enforcement. Who audits what institutions actually do, and who pulls the funder lever if NIH doesn't. I still don't have that answer.

Kenneth put stop counting papers first, and the room agreed. What worried me is how easily "funders stop counting" turned into another declaration. I said enforcement out loud: public misconduct reports by default, retraction notices that say whether anyone investigated, audit power for ORI or whoever replaces it. James's point hit hardest. A checkers' guild made of senior reviewers rebuilds the lamp post, and I've watched gatekeepers protect themselves for fifteen years. Henry's "don't moan, organize" answers the sleuth question I'd been circling since this morning.

Where I sharpened: correction speed is my metric, and Goodhart applies to it. I said so this time.

Still unanswered: who pays as a last resort. Foundations came and went for Retraction Watch. An endowment, not goodwill.
